assessment.nobel_worthiness: A clean theory-to-experiment story: the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model predicted flat bands at a magic twist angle, and the 2018 observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene opened moire quantum matter as a whole new platform. Strongly correlated electrons with tunable parameters is a statistical-physics problem of broad reach, and the field has spread to many materials.
assessment.attribution: Theory (Bistritzer and MacDonald) and the decisive experiment (Jarillo-Herrero and collaborators) form a natural three-person configuration. Credit for the experiment may reasonably extend to co-authors outside the supplied names, and the supplied list may not match every committee view of who is decisive.
assessment.maturity: Roughly eight years of intense, independently reproduced work across many groups; the basic phenomenology is stable. Recognition is timely, though mechanisms of the superconductivity remain debated.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism of superconductivity in twisted graphene is not settled.
Whether the prize is best framed around the theory prediction, the experiment, or the broader moire field is open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised Hubbard-type models with controllable parameters, observed the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopy. This is a direct bridge between many-body statistical physics and controllable experiment, and it has influenced condensed matter, quantum information and non-equilibrium dynamics.
assessment.attribution: The field has too many leaders for three slots. Zoller's theoretical proposals, Bloch's experiments and Greiner's microscopy are the most distinctive within the supplied names, but Cirac, Esslinger and others have strong claims, and a fair split is hard.
assessment.maturity: Mature: more than twenty years of confirmation and many replications. Recognition is somewhat overdue, and the 2001 and 2012 prizes on cold atoms and single quantum systems partly overlap in subject.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier atomic-physics prizes may reduce novelty.
Allocation among Bloch, Esslinger, Greiner, Zoller and Cirac is genuinely contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction and fault tolerance showed that large-scale quantum computation is in principle possible despite noise; topological codes tie it to many-body physics. Conceptually foundational and now directly guiding experiments.
assessment.attribution: Shor (first code and fault-tolerance ideas) and Kitaev (toric code, anyons) are the decisive figures in the supplied names; Steane's independent code construction is also important. A threshold-theorem co-credit (not in the supplied names) complicates a clean allocation.
assessment.maturity: The theory is mature, and experimental demonstrations of logical qubits below threshold are emerging but still early. Recognition is plausible and increasingly timely.
uncertainties: Experimental validation of scalable fault tolerance is still incomplete.
Whether this is physics, computer science or mathematics for prize purposes may be debated.
Credit for the threshold theorem includes people outside the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Intermittency and multifractal structure of turbulence concern a century-old problem and tie directly to my own field of statistical physics of fluids and particles in flows. Frisch's multifractal framework and Sreenivasan's experimental scaling work shaped the modern view of anomalous scaling and its relation to Kolmogorov theory.
assessment.attribution: Frisch and Sreenivasan are plausible representatives, but important roles by Parisi, Kolmogorov, Kraichnan, Benzi and others complicate attribution. Both named people made distinctive contributions, but neither supplies a single decisive discovery.
assessment.maturity: The phenomenology of anomalous scaling is well confirmed, but a first-principles theory of intermittency is lacking, so the interpretation is incomplete. Prizes for this area are rare because of that maturity gap.
uncertainties: The multifractal model is phenomenological, and the underlying theory of turbulence remains unresolved.
A bias from my own research area should be acknowledged and discounted.
Credit distribution across a wide field is unclear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The jamming transition unified rigidity and disorder in granular matter, foams and glasses with a critical-phenomena viewpoint. It is an original, conceptually clear idea in soft matter and complex systems with a growing set of theoretical and experimental confirmations.
assessment.attribution: Liu and Nagel proposed the jamming phase diagram together, which gives a clean two-person attribution; others (O'Hern, Silbert, Wyart, Parisi and Zamponi) contributed important later theory.
assessment.maturity: About twenty-five years old, with solid numerical and some experimental support. Mean-field theory connections are developing; the critical scaling picture is largely accepted but the real-world applicability to finite-temperature glasses is debated.
uncertainties: Experimental tests in real granular systems are less clean than simulations.
Possible overlap with the 2021 recognition of complex systems and the glass problem.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Time-reversal-invariant topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect created a new classification of electronic matter and prompted a vast research programme. Theoretical originality is high and experimental confirmation was swift.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the theoretical prediction, and Molenkamp's group observed the effect in HgTe wells (proposed by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who are outside the supplied names). This leaves a real allocation problem, as well as the question of the 2016 prize's overlap.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and widely confirmed, though application impact is still limited. The 2016 prize on topological phases weakens the case for further recognition.
uncertainties: The HgTe proposal credit (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) is not among the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Direct horizon-scale images of M87* and Sgr A* are a technical and scientific milestone, giving test data for strong-field gravity. The images are striking, but the physical conclusions are largely model-dependent.
assessment.attribution: The EHT is a very large collaboration, and attribution to three people is unavoidably a simplification. Falcke (shadow concept), Doeleman (VLBI technique and leadership) and Moran (mm-VLBI) are plausible, but a collaboration-wide prize is not possible under the statutes.
assessment.maturity: Recent (2019 and 2022); confirmation by repeated epochs and polarisation results is improving, but independent verification from other facilities is limited. Timing is arguably early.
uncertainties: Interpretations depend on general-relativistic MHD simulation choices.
Allocation across a large collaboration is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks at the 10^-18 level are a precision-measurement milestone enabling tests of fundamental physics, geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice idea and Ye's demonstrations of record stability are clear and important.
assessment.attribution: Katori (the lattice clock proposal) and Ye (record precision and many-body clocks) form a natural two-person attribution. Others in ion clocks and optical-frequency combs have been recognised by earlier prizes, so attribution is relatively clean.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently reproduced in several laboratories; the redefinition of the second is still pending, so the societal impact is not yet realised. Timing is reasonable.
uncertainties: Overlap in subject with the 2005 and 2012 prizes on frequency combs and trapped ions.
Roles of other groups (e.g. Hollberg, Ludlow) are not in the supplied names.
